package_info.package_manager: N/A (custom exploit tool, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: Affects all supported Windows versions (Windows 10/11, fully patched as of 2024-10)
package_info.why_malicious: The tool enables attackers to downgrade critical Windows system components (such as ci.dll, drivers, and kernel modules) to older, vulnerable versions by bypassing Windows file protection and update mechanisms. This reintroduces patched vulnerabilities, allows unsigned or malicious kernel drivers to be loaded, disables security features, and facilitates further malicious activity while evading detection and maintaining persistence.

execution_context.file_location: ci.dll (Windows Code Integrity module), other system DLLs/drivers

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Downdate tool logic: Overwrite patched system DLL (e.g., ci.dll) with an older, vulnerable version, bypassing Windows file protection and update mechanisms.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the tool overwrites a patched system DLL (such as ci.dll) with an older, vulnerable version by bypassing Windows file protection and update mechanisms, resulting in the reintroduction of previously patched vulnerabilities and the circumvention of digital signature enforcement.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Overwriting protected system files with outdated, vulnerable versions is a well-known privilege escalation and persistence technique that directly undermines the integrity of the operating system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal system operation expects system DLLs to be immutable and only updated through trusted Windows Update mechanisms. Downgrading to vulnerable versions outside of these channels is never legitimate and breaks the security model.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate system recovery or rollback tools may restore previous versions, but only with explicit user or administrator consent, proper logging, and through official recovery workflows.
key_indicators: Direct replacement of system DLLs (e.g., ci.dll) with older versions outside of Windows Update
Bypassing Windows file protection and digital signature enforcement mechanisms
Presence of system files with known-vulnerable hashes or timestamps inconsistent with expected baselines

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Exploit logic: Trigger page faults to force Windows to reload and allow modification of files marked as immutable, exploiting 'False File Immutability' (ItsNotASecurityBoundary).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the exploit triggers page faults in the kernel to force Windows to reload protected files and exploit the 'False File Immutability' flaw, allowing modification of files that should be immutable, which enables further exploitation and persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Bypassing file immutability to modify protected system files is a direct exploitation of a security boundary and is indicative of malicious intent to subvert OS protections.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Protected system files are expected to be locked and unmodifiable after being secured by the OS. Exploiting page fault handling to alter them is highly abnormal and not permitted in legitimate workflows.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use for exploiting page faults to modify protected files; this technique is exclusively used for malicious purposes.
key_indicators: Triggering page faults in the kernel to modify protected files
Modifying files with write access explicitly denied by the OS
Targeting system files that have been patched for known vulnerabilities

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Load unsigned kernel driver: Use the downgraded, vulnerable ci.dll to load an unsigned or malicious kernel driver.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after downgrading ci.dll, the attacker loads an unsigned or malicious kernel driver by exploiting the vulnerable code integrity checks, bypassing digital signature enforcement and enabling arbitrary code execution in kernel mode.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading unsigned drivers on a fully patched system is a major red flag, as it bypasses core Windows security controls and enables attackers to execute arbitrary code with kernel privileges.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Windows is designed to only allow signed drivers to be loaded, especially on systems with Secure Boot and Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) enabled. Loading unsigned drivers after a suspicious DLL downgrade is never legitimate.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate driver development or testing may require test signing, but this is only done on non-production systems with explicit configuration and is never performed on production endpoints without proper controls.
key_indicators: Loading of unsigned or test-signed drivers on systems with Secure Boot and DSE enabled
Driver loads occurring immediately after suspicious DLL downgrades
Kernel-level code execution without valid digital signatures

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains administrative or SYSTEM-level access to the target Windows system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to execute custom tools and modify system files

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses the Downdate tool to overwrite patched system DLLs (e.g., ci.dll) with older, vulnerable versions.
attack_chain.leads_to: System is now running with known-vulnerable components

attack_chain.action: Attacker exploits 'False File Immutability' by triggering page faults to modify protected files, bypassing write restrictions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Further modification of system files and persistence

attack_chain.action: Attacker loads unsigned or malicious kernel drivers using the downgraded ci.dll, bypassing digital signature enforcement.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full kernel-level code execution, disabling security features, deploying rootkits, etc.

attack_chain.action: Attacker disables security features, deploys and disguises malicious code and processes, and maintains persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: complete system compromise and evasion of detection

behavioral_signatures: Unexplained downgrades of system DLLs or drivers to older, vulnerable versions outside of Windows Update
Modification of protected system files (such as ci.dll) without use of official update mechanisms
Loading of unsigned or test-signed kernel drivers on Secure Boot-enabled systems
Unusual page fault activity correlated with modifications to protected system files
file_indicators: ci.dll or other core system DLLs replaced with older, known-vulnerable versions
Timestamps or cryptographic hashes of system files not matching expected values from official baselines
Presence of custom tools or scripts capable of DLL/driver replacement in system directories
network_indicators: Outbound connections for downloading old or vulnerable DLLs or drivers from non-Microsoft sources
Potential command-and-control (C2) traffic if malicious drivers establish persistence or exfiltrate data
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor for changes to system DLLs and drivers, especially downgrades to known-vulnerable versions. Alert on any modification of protected files outside of Windows Update or official recovery workflows. Detect and alert on attempts to load unsigned or test-signed drivers on systems with Secure Boot or Driver Signature Enforcement enabled. Correlate abnormal page fault activity with file modifications on protected system files. Employ file integrity monitoring and maintain a baseline of expected system file versions and hashes to detect unauthorized changes.
